processes: Sorting triangles by sides and angles
plainLanguageExplanation: A triangle is a closed shape made of three straight segments joined at three vertices. It has three sides, three corners, and three interior angles — and no matter what the triangle looks like, those angles always add up to exactly 180°. Triangles come in families: by sides — equilateral (all equal), isosceles (two equal), scalene (none equal); by angles — acute, right, obtuse. A triangle is also the only polygon that can't be pushed out of shape — it is rigid, which is why bridges and roofs use triangles everywhere.

keyFacts.label: Rigid
keyFacts.value: Cannot be pushed out of shape

whyItMatters: Triangles are the strongest and most common shape in engineering — roof trusses, bridge frames, bike frames, and cranes all use triangles because they refuse to flex. They are also the first shape students learn to measure and the foundation of all polygons.
didYouKnow: Because a triangle's three sides lock its angles, it is the only polygon that holds its shape under pressure — that is why the world's strongest structures are full of triangles.
compareReason: Students think all closed shapes behave alike — comparing the rigid triangle with the flexible quadrilateral shows the unique strength.
